processes.description: Employees file expense reports through Concur (one request names Enron's XMS system). Concur emails the approver that a report is ready for approval and later that its approval status has changed; the approver reviews the items and approves or rejects them. Assistants also ask colleagues for outstanding items to be expensed, and during the bankruptcy announcements push approvers to clear reports waiting in their inboxes and explain which bills fall under pre-petition.
steps: An employee or assistant gathers outstanding invoices and receipts to be expensed.
The expense report is filed in the Concur expense system.
Concur notifies the approver that the report is ready for approval.
The approver reviews the items and approves or rejects the report.
Concur notifies the submitter that the approval status has changed.
The expenses are reimbursed, with bills treated according to whether they were submitted before the pre-petition cutoff.

stalls.summary: A submitter cannot get into the expense system and asks for help with the Concur login and password, so the report waits until access is restored.

Reports sit unprocessed: an announcement asks approvers to either approve or reject the outstanding business expenses in their inboxes, and staff are asked to file the outstanding employee expenses they hold as soon as possible.

contradictions.summary: One announcement says expenses will be reimbursed promptly upon submission, while another sorts bills by whether they were submitted before a mid-December date and treats those as covered under pre-petition, so the treatment of an item depends on when it was submitted.

automation.approach: A daily report from the expense system listing reports awaiting approval by approver and age, with automatic reminders, plus rule checks that flag items missing receipts, outside policy, or on the wrong side of the pre-petition cutoff so approvers look closely only at flagged items. Self-service password reset would remove the login stall.
automation.rationale: The system already routes reports, so the remaining hands-on work is the approver's review and the submitter's gathering of invoices. A short checklist covering what to attach, the bankruptcy cutoff rules and how to regain system access would reduce rejected and stuck reports soonest; the queue report addresses reports left sitting in inboxes.

work_estimate.rationale: Most rounds are one report: the approver opens it in Concur, checks the line items and receipts against policy and approves or rejects it, a few minutes for a routine report, so mid 8 minutes. Some rounds instead have a submitter collect outstanding invoices or bills and file them, which takes longer and sets the upper end near 20 minutes. Routing is already automated; rule checks could take over part of the item review.

processes.description: Customers and suppliers such as Calpine, Enron Methanol and TXU send daily or monthly gas nominations, often as attached forms or spreadsheets. Schedulers enter the volumes in Sitara, set them up on the right contract and pipeline, and confirm. Revised nominations follow whenever volumes change, including retroactive changes that are checked against the contracts and corrected; traders and plant contacts forward changes such as plant swings or buybacks to be renominated, and the gas is then tracked and balanced.
steps: A customer or supplier sends a daily or monthly nomination, often as an attached form or spreadsheet.
The scheduler checks the request against the contract and the transport arrangements.
Estimated or nominated volumes are entered in Sitara on the right contract and meter.
The nomination is placed with the pipeline and confirmed back to the requester.
When volumes change, a revised nomination arrives and is forwarded to the scheduler responsible.
The scheduler updates the volumes, including retroactive corrections, and settles how any buyback is priced.
The gas is tracked and balanced against the nominated volumes.

stalls.summary: Schedulers wait on counterparties and colleagues: a supplier is still waiting on a transport number, a request goes unanswered until a follow-up asks whether it was checked, and an update waits on a returned phone call.

Volumes are changed repeatedly: a customer drops the volume again, another asks for a nomination to show zero, a supplier revises its nom for a span of days, and a scheduler corrects noms entered wrongly at the start of the month.
Customers request nomination changes retroactive to earlier dates, and management warns that retroactive deals affect daily operations and that contracts must be reviewed and understood.
An attachment with the full month position keeps bouncing off the mail gateway, so the position is pasted into the message body instead.
Nomination work is spread across several people, prompting a suggestion to centralize transport nominations and a later assignment of off-system nominations to one scheduler.

contradictions.summary: Volumes on the books disagree with what counterparties want: a customer is looking for a different February volume at a meter than nominated, another asks for a nomination to show zero instead, and a scheduler finds the noms entered at the start of the month were a mistake.

automation.approach: Standard nomination intake: counterparties submit a fixed spreadsheet layout that a tool reads into Sitara, compares with the previous nomination and the contract, and flags changed volumes, retroactive dates and missing transport numbers for the scheduler before the confirmation goes out. A shared list of nomination owners by pipeline routes each change to one person.
automation.rationale: Nominations arrive as Word forms, spreadsheets and pasted text, and much of the hands-on work is re-keying and comparing volumes. One nomination template that every counterparty fills in makes entry and comparison mechanical, leaving schedulers the judgement on retroactive changes, pricing and contract fit.

work_estimate.rationale: Minutes go to reading the nomination form, checking it against the contract and transport, entering or changing volumes in Sitara and confirming with the pipeline. A routine daily nom sits near the low end of 10 minutes; revised or retroactive changes that need contract review, correction of earlier entries and rebalancing push toward 60 minutes. Mid 20 minutes reflects the mix of routine noms and revisions.

processes.description: Staff on the trading side explain, enter and revise internal annuities that move revenue between books, such as profit sharing on a deal split between two desks. A round starts with a request to revise an annuity, a question about an unexplained beginning-of-month charge before month-end, or a note listing annuities entered to reconcile counterparty records with Enpower; the reply names the books involved and attaches a supporting spreadsheet.
steps: A request arrives to explain or revise an internal annuity, or a prior-month charge is queried.
The deal and the books the revenue moves between are looked up.
The split and its basis are explained, with a supporting spreadsheet attached.
The annuity is entered or revised.
Annuities are entered to reconcile counterparty records with Enpower before month-end.

stalls.summary: Annuities already booked have to be revised, and unexplained beginning-of-month charges are queried before month-end, so the same deals come round again.

contradictions.summary: Counterparty records and Enpower disagree for a past year, and annuities are entered specifically to bring the two into line.

automation.approach: A standard annuity record kept with each deal: the books moved from and to, the split, the reason and the period, plus a month-end check that compares Enpower with counterparty records and lists differences and unexplained charges before P&L closes.
automation.rationale: Explanations are rebuilt from memory and an older spreadsheet, so one layout per annuity would let anyone answer revision questions and reconcile records without depending on the person who first booked it.
